title: What the homepage has to prove for a fintech product
metaTitle: Fintech product homepage: product, people, path
excerpt: A fintech homepage has to show the product in a real state, name the people responsible, and offer a way to open an account or talk to sales.
alt: A pale beach at sunrise, with small waves washing onto the sand and palm trees in the distance, a quiet first frame for a page that has to be clear before it asks for money.
caption: Sunrise on a pale beach. The first screen should be this calm, and this specific. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a fintech homepage show first?
faqs.answer: Show the product in a state a customer recognizes, then the people or entity responsible for it, then one way to start an account or talk to sales. A buyer deciding whether to move money needs those three things before a slogan. If the first screen is only adjectives about safety, the page has not started the job.

faqs.question: Should a fintech homepage hide pricing until a sales call?
faqs.answer: No. The homepage does not need the full rate card, but it should show the shape of the price if a buyer will ask anyway. A monthly platform fee, a per-transaction fee, or a line that says pricing depends on volume is a shape. A page that says nothing until a form is filled teaches people the site is a brochure.

faqs.question: Where should security claims live on the homepage?
faqs.answer: Put a short, checkable fact near the product, and keep the long note for a page that can hold it. A claim you can point at, such as who holds funds or who reviews an exception, belongs where the buyer is already looking. A padlock icon and a sentence about DNA do not answer the question.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A fintech product homepage has one job for a buyer who may hand the company money. Show the product in a real state, name the people responsible for it, and offer a way to start an account or talk to sales.

Abstract trust language fails that buyer. Lines about bank-grade peace of mind do not show a balance, a transfer, or a person who answers when something goes wrong. Write the page in that order: product, people, path.

## Show the product before you praise it

The first screen is a product shot with a sentence, not a manifesto. A buyer who needs to trust a company with money is looking for the thing they will use. A balance. A card. A payout. A ledger. A pending review. If they cannot point at it, they will not stay for the adjectives.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on page visits is blunt about the clock. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. A page earns several minutes of attention only when the value is clear inside about 10 seconds. On a money product, that value is the product itself. Put a real interface in the frame. Use a state a customer recognizes, not an empty dashboard with round numbers that look invented.

Write one sentence under the picture that says who it is for and what changes. "Payouts for marketplaces that already have sellers" is a sentence. "The future of finance" is a mood. The sentence should still make sense if the picture fails to load.

Keep the type quiet. A homepage that shouts competes with the product. Hanabi's public product work, including Got Next and Leadly, is a reminder that one screen and one hierarchy read faster than a collage of features. You do not need their subject matter. You need the restraint. One job on the screen. Words that say what happens next.

If the product has more than one job, pick the job this buyer came for. A homepage that tries to be a card, a treasury tool, and a lending desk at once asks the visitor to sort your company before they understand it. Secondary jobs can live further down, each with its own sentence. The first screen gets one.

## Name the people responsible

Money is a relationship with a person, even when the product is software. The homepage should say who stands behind the account. That can be a short line. The regulated entity. The team that reviews exceptions. The named contact for a certain size of customer. It should be a name or a role a buyer can repeat, not "our team of experts."

Google's guidance on helpful content treats trust as the center of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness. It gives extra weight to topics that can affect someone's financial stability. A homepage is not a research paper, but the same test applies. A visitor should be able to tell who is offering the product. If the only name on the page is the product name, you have asked them to trust a logo.

Place that line near the product, not in a footer essay. A portrait helps when it is a real person in a real room, doing a job the buyer understands. A stock smile next to a padlock does the opposite. It signals that the company could not show its own people.

If you are regulated, say the true thing in plain words. The license. The partner bank. The country. The thing you do not hold. Do not decorate it. A buyer who needs the fact will look for it. A buyer who does not need it yet should still see that you were willing to write it down. Hiding the entity until the application form is a way to spend the buyer's patience on a surprise.

## One path: open an account or talk to sales

The page needs one next step, written as the buyer would say it. For some products that is opening an account. For others it is a sales conversation. Pick the path that matches how you actually take a customer. A homepage with both, plus a demo video, a waitlist, and a newsletter, is a page that has not chosen.

The button should sit where the product sentence ends. Repeat it after the proof, in the same words. If opening an account takes documents, say so beside the button in one line. A government ID and a business address, stated early, is kinder than a surprise on screen three of a form.

If the real next step is a conversation, the button should book that conversation, and the line under it should say what the call is for. Fit. The shape of the price. Whether this buyer is in range. It is not a tour of the roadmap, and it should not be labeled as one.

Two honest paths are allowed when they are truly different buyers. "Open an account" for a self-serve plan and "Talk to sales" for a volume plan can sit side by side if the labels say who each one is for. Two buttons that go to the same form are noise. So is a third button that says "Learn more" and scrolls to another slogan.

## Why abstract trust language fails

Teams reach for abstract trust language because the product feels risky and the homepage feels like the place to soothe that risk. The language soothes the team. It does not help the buyer who has to move money.

Lines that fail a simple test:

- "Your money is safe with us."
- "Built on trust."
- "Security is in our DNA."
- "A new standard for finance."
- "Seamless, powerful, and secure."

None of these show a product state or a person. They also tend to occupy the first sentence, so the buyer spends the opening seconds decoding a mood. Nielsen's point is practical here. If the value is not clear quickly, you do not get the later minutes in which a real security note could have been read.

Replace each line with a concrete one. "Transfers settle the same business day to a linked account" can be checked. "We do not sell customer transaction data" can be checked. "Exceptions are reviewed by a person on the support desk" can be checked. If you cannot check it, do not put it in the first screen. A longer security page can hold the nuance. The homepage holds the fact a buyer needs in order to continue.

Watch the words your own team uses in the hallway. "Compliant," "enterprise-grade," and "trusted by operators" often sneak back in during a design review because they feel safer than a specific sentence. Safer for the writer. Harder for the buyer. Read the headline out loud and ask what a stranger could verify. If the answer is nothing, rewrite the line before you debate the type size.

## Write the page in that order

Keep this order when the layout gets polished. Decoration should not be allowed to reshuffle it.

1. The product in a real state, with one sentence on who it is for.
2. The people responsible, including the regulated fact if there is one.
3. The path: start an account or talk to sales.
4. Two or three specifics a buyer will ask anyway: the price shape, what you hold, what you do not do.
5. One proof story with a constraint and a decision, not a row of unnamed logos.
6. The path again, in the same words.

Do not open with a manifesto, a funding announcement, or a carousel of industries. Those are for people who already decided to stay. The first screen is for people who have not.

A second screen can carry the fee shape in one line, even when a full pricing page exists. Hiding every number until a sales call teaches the buyer that the site is a gate. If the price is custom, say the true shape. Priced by volume. A monthly platform fee plus a per-payout fee. A percentage with a floor. The spreadsheet can live one click away. The shape belongs here, because this is where the buyer decides whether to keep reading.

Proof, when you have it, is one story. A customer type, a constraint, and what you decided. A logo bar with no sentence asks the visitor to imagine the rest. Imagined proof is not proof. If you are early and the honest proof is the product and the named people, stop there. Do not borrow credibility from a client list you cannot explain.

## What to remove from the first screen

Cut anything that does not serve the product, the people, or the path.

- A video that plays before the product is readable.
- A header with twelve destinations.
- Three headlines stacked on one image.
- Partner logos with no sentence.
- A chat bubble that covers the button.
- Motion that moves the account button while the page settles.

The last item is a product decision, not a polish pass. A buyer came to see the product and take the path. If the layout jumps after the hero image arrives, the page has argued with them. On a Hanabi marketing site the build is Next.js, with type and layout in Tailwind, and motion only where it helps a person understand. On a money homepage, the helpful motion is usually none. Reduced motion is part of finishing the page, not a setting you remember after launch.

Also cut the internal vocabulary. "Rails," "ledgering," "orchestration," and "program management" may be how the team talks. They are not how a first-time buyer asks for the job. Translate the noun into the outcome, then use the internal word on a page for people who already know it. The homepage is not that page.

## Review it the way a buyer will

Read the first screen on a phone, out loud, to someone who does not work at the company. Ask three questions. What is the product? Who is responsible? What do I do next? If any answer is a paraphrase of "they seem trustworthy," the page is not done.

Then read the fee line and the security line as a skeptical buyer. Every claim should be visible in the product, written as a fact, or removed. Google's people-first questions are a useful second pass. Would someone who came to you directly learn enough to take the next step, and can they tell who created this? A homepage that only works as a search ad fails that test.

When you want that standard applied to your own first screen, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current page and one real product state. The call should tell you whether the homepage can be rewritten in place or needs a clearer product story before any layout work.

The next decision is the page this buyer opens after they believe you. [A pricing page for a fintech product](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-fintech-product) is about showing what is included, what is not, and the shape of the price without turning the visit into a puzzle.
